title: Namdev and the Dog
hookLine: a saint chases a thief with butter, and a temple turns around
carry: the same Lord in the dog and the priest
tomorrow: Why would a saint split his last stalk with the wife who hit him?

cards: Lunch is laid out: a few pieces of flatbread, and a little pot of ghee, clarified butter, to spread on top. Namdev looks away for a moment. A stray dog trots in, snatches the bread, and runs.
Namdev jumps up and goes after it. Not with a stick. He's carrying the pot of ghee, calling: wait, that bread is dry, let me butter it for you.
That's the story told about him.

teach.b: Visoba taught Namdev that there's no place without God. Here is that lesson trotting off on four legs. In the story, Namdev sees Vitthal in the dog, and the one problem left is that the bread is dry.
Namdev goes to a temple to sing; tradition places it at Aundha. The priests push him out. In their eyes, a man of his birth doesn't belong there.
So Namdev walks around to the back, sits on the ground, and keeps singing. And the story says the temple turned, the whole building swinging around until its door faced Namdev.

teach.h: A HYMN IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.
teach.b: Namdev tells this one himself, in a hymn kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs: driven out for the community he was born into, he sang, and the temple turned to face him.

Put the two stories side by side, and you have one of Hinduism's great teachings. The Bhagavad Gita says the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the one the world calls an outcast.

teach.h: THE EQUAL EYE: ONE LORD IN EVERY BEING.
teach.b: Teachers call it sama-darshana, the equal eye: one Lord living in every being. Namdev lived both halves of that verse.
He saw God in the dog, and the story says God would not keep his back to a singer the priests saw as less.
It's part of why many Hindu homes, especially in north India, still set aside the first roti for a cow and the last for a dog. The hungry animal at the door isn't outside the sacred.

how: Varkari devotees in Maharashtra sing Namdev's songs to Vitthal, and Sikhs read and sing the hymns under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib. Many Hindu homes, especially in north India, set aside the first roti for a cow and the last for a dog.

games.q: a hungry dog runs off with your lunch. you've learned Namdev's lesson, the equal eye. what do you see?
o: a thief to chase off with a stick.
Vitthal, with nothing on his bread.
a sign of bad luck for the day.
games.why: Namdev saw the Lord in the dog and chased it with ghee. the Gita's equal eye sees one Lord in every being.

practice: Before your next meal, set a little aside, the way many Hindu homes keep a roti for the cow and one for the dog: a bite of bread, a handful of rice.
Put it out for a bird or a neighbor's dog, or into the hands of someone who needs it. As you do, think of someone who annoyed you lately: the same Lord lives there too.
If you pray, offer the food to God first; if you don't, simply give it with care.
